title: Teaching SQL with an Agentic LLM: A Fifteen-Category Hallucination Taxonomy and Context-Pack Mitigation Strategy for Claude Sonnet 5
content: Text-to-SQL generation with large language models (LLMs) is increasingly used in database teaching, yet it remains susceptible to hallucination: the production of syntactically valid but referentially or semantically incorrect queries. This paper proposes a working taxonomy of fifteen hallucination categories in text-to-SQL generation, spanning schema-referential errors, join and cardinality errors, aggregation-grain errors, linguistic ambiguity, dialect and type misuse, NULL and temporal-logic errors, and higher-order failure modes such as explanation-query inconsistency, fabricated execu- tion results, and false security assumptions. Each category is illustrated with a natural-language request and a corresponding hallucinated query against a common PostgreSQL schema, together with a targeted mitigation. Mitigations are organized into two complementary layers: a context pack supplied once by the instructor (schema DDL, column catalog, foreign-key graph, and a set of standing rules) and an agentic execute-observe-correct loop, formalized here through explicit definitions of "generation" and "session", in which an assistant such as Claude Sonnet 5 issues queries against a live PostgreSQL database via the Model Context Protocol (MCP), inspects the returned rows or errors, and revises the query before presenting it to the user. The paper provides a recap table of categories and countermeasures, intended as a practical checklist for instructors and students applying agentic LLMs to SQL laboratory training. The taxonomy is positioned against related error classifications from the text-to-SQL and broader LLM-hallucination literature, showing convergence on schema- and logic-level categories while identifying conversational and pedagogical failure modes – ambiguity, car- dinality fan-out, explanation inconsistency, fabricated results, and security over-confidence – that fall outside the scope of static, benchmark-based taxonomies. The paper argues that the fifteen categories are structural properties of schema-grounded SQL generation and therefore model-agnostic, while their frequency and severity are expected to vary across model tiers and context pack quality. The paper concludes by highlighting three avenues for future research: extending the empirical material to schemas of realistic industrial scale; a classroom deployment study comparing learning outcomes with and without the proposed mitigations; and a sampling-based characterization of hallucination frequency and robustness across repeated and adversarial prompting.
